name: geo-utils-cpp
baseline: Boost.Geometry 1.90 (spherical_equatorial strategy: bg::within and bg::area); also S2 Geometry 0.14.0 and GeographicLib 2.7
workload: Google Benchmark on seeded random lat/lng data: spherical point-in-polygon (polygons of 10, 100 and 1000 vertices, 1000 query points per iteration) and spherical polygon area (10/100/1000 vertices); native library types are built outside the timed loop.
claimed_speedup: contains (M queries/s, geo-utils-cpp vs Boost.Geometry): 16.2 vs 1.91 at N=10, 2.87 vs 0.234 at N=100, 0.329 vs 0.024 at N=1000 (about 8.5x, 12x and 14x, derived from page data). area (M polygons/s): 69.9 vs 45.0 at N=10, 67.2 vs 36.2 at N=100, 67.7 vs 36.6 at N=1000 (about 1.5-1.9x, derived from page data). distance_between and heading tie Boost.Geometry within noise.
compiler_and_flags: Apple clang 17, -std=c++17 -O2 -DNDEBUG, Release, Google Benchmark 1.8.4, Boost 1.90.0
hardware: Apple M1, 8 cores, 8 GB RAM, macOS 15.7
tradeoffs: Header-only, no dependencies, lat/lng-native API. Spherical Earth only (mean radius 6371009 m), not WGS84 ellipsoidal; accuracy degrades near the poles and for antipodal pairs. Far smaller feature set than Boost.Geometry (no generic geometry types, no spatial index).
caveats: The contains comparison is not like for like: geo-utils-cpp uses an O(N) ray cast over rhumb-line edges while bg::within with the spherical CS picks a great-circle winding strategy, so the 8-14x gap partly reflects algorithm choice (the docs say so). S2 beats it by a wide margin on contains (18.0 M/s at N=100) and on distance at small N. Single machine (Apple M1, clang) only, no GCC/MSVC or x86 numbers. Young repo (commits visible from May 2026).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/geospatial?l=c++ and WebSearch 'faster than GEOS C++ library spatial github'

name: Delaunay32
baseline: Triangle 1.6 (also Fade2D 2.17.3, delaunator-cpp, CDT 1.4.5); CGAL not compared
workload: 2D Delaunay triangulation of one million unique, unconstrained int32 points, triangle-only output, runtime in ms.
claimed_speedup: Delaunay32 1 thread 131.6 ms and 8 threads 45.4 ms versus Triangle 1.6 584.0 ms, Fade2D 2.17.3 314.1 ms (1 thread) / 235.2 ms (automatic threads), delaunator-cpp 542.0 ms, CDT 1.4.5 988.7 ms (README table; single-thread about 4.4x over Triangle, derived from page data).
tradeoffs: Core API accepts only signed 32-bit integer coordinates; float input must go through an explicit quantize() step that can collide points. Exact integer predicates, constraints and polygon domains with holes, serial or shared-memory parallel. No bundled third-party sources. Triangle-only output is the default.
caveats: Own README table only (one 1M-point uniform case on one machine, compiler and flags not stated), though benchmark sources ship in the repo (delaunay_benchmark). CGAL, the category incumbent, is not in the comparison, so Triangle is the nearest widely used baseline. Fade2D is commercial. Benchmark compares an integer-exact kernel against floating-point libraries, so work done per point differs. Very young repo (commits visible from August 2026).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/delaunay-triangulation?l=c++ and WebSearch 'C++ Delaunay triangulation library faster than CGAL benchmark github'

name: clipper2next
baseline: Clipper2 (AngusJohnson/Clipper2, called 'legacy Clipper2' in the README)
workload: Integer polygon boolean ops (intersection, union, difference, XOR), offsetting, triangulation, Minkowski, rect clip and PolyTree on an external benchmark corpus of 11 normalized profiles (2,426 cases); results first compared exactly against legacy Clipper2 with no coordinate tolerance.
claimed_speedup: Linux (GCC 13.1, -O3) vs legacy Clipper2: 14-pair geometric mean 1.615x; intersection 1.584x, union 1.669x, difference 1.694x, XOR 1.715x, offset 1.770x, triangulation 2.340x, Minkowski 1.454x. Windows (MSVC 19.44 /O2) geometric mean 1.758x, labelled directional because of variance (intersection 1.487x, offset 1.563x, triangulation 2.878x).
compiler_and_flags: Linux: GCC 13.1 -O3 -DNDEBUG; Windows: MSVC 19.44 /O2 /Ob2 /DNDEBUG; Google Benchmark 1.9.5, 7 repetitions of at least 0.5 s, pairwise process isolation, randomized pair order, 1 s warmup, 5% CV ceiling
tradeoffs: Requires C++23 (std::expected), CMake 3.24 and Ninja; integer (Point64) geometry only, like Clipper2. Keeps Clipper2's result contract (strict equivalence) while adding prepared requests, borrowed input ranges, flat path sets and streaming topology output. The README says 6.x makes no new speedup claim.
caveats: CPU model is not stated anywhere I could open, so this falls short of tier A. All numbers are the author's own against the author's chosen 'legacy' Clipper2 build, and the speedups depend on the API (default/unprepared calls). Windows result flagged noisy by the author. Repo is about four weeks old (first commit 2026-09-03), one star, and the README does not say how much of the source derives from Clipper2 (GitHub does not mark it as a fork). Baseline Clipper2 is not Boost.Geometry/GEOS/CGAL; no comparison against those.
found_via: WebSearch 'C++ polygon boolean union intersection library github benchmark Boost.Geometry Clipper speedup times faster'

name: PicoTree
baseline: nanoflann v1.7.1 (also OpenCV FLANN 4.11.0, SciPy KDTree, scikit-learn KDTree, pykdtree)
workload: KdTree build and 1-nearest-neighbor query over two LiDAR point clouds of 7,733,372 points (build) and 7,200,863 points (query), single thread, max_leaf_size=10, knn=1.
claimed_speedup: C++ build 0.54 s vs nanoflann 1.42 s vs OpenCV FLANN 0.99 s; C++ knn 1.13 s vs nanoflann 1.40 s vs OpenCV FLANN 2.30 s. Python: build 0.54 s vs pykdtree 0.43 s (slower) vs SciPy 1.37 s vs scikit-learn 3.60 s; knn 1.64 s vs pykdtree 2.95 s, SciPy 212.04 s, scikit-learn 11.90 s. About 2.6x faster build and 1.24x faster knn than nanoflann (derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the README table; docs/benchmark.md (older run, PicoTree v0.7.4 vs nanoflann v1.3.2) used MinGW GCC 10.3
tradeoffs: Header-only with Python (pybind11) bindings; exact NN, radius and box searches; Eigen and OpenCV adapters. Covers kd-tree searches only (no R-tree, no polygon or mesh operations).
caveats: README table has no compiler or flags and is the author's own run; benchmark code lives under examples/benchmark but the table's build setup is not documented in the README. The knn gain over nanoflann is modest (about 1.2x); the build gain is larger. The author notes nanoflann's build regressed (90% slower in v1.5.0) in an older comparison, so the build ratio depends on the nanoflann version. Baseline nanoflann is already catalogued separately, and is not Boost.Geometry/CGAL/GEOS.

name: jc_voronoi
baseline: Boost.Polygon voronoi_diagram (also Fastjet/Fortune C, O'Sullivan C++, voronoi++)
workload: 2D Voronoi diagram generation from point sets (Fortune sweep), time and memory, minimum of 20 runs per test.
claimed_speedup: README 'General thoughts': Boost is '~2x as slow as the fastest algorithms, and takes ~2.5x as much memory'; voronoi++ is 10x-15x slower. The timing, memory and allocation charts (test/images/*.png) were not retrievable, so no per-size numbers.
hardware: Intel Core i7-7567U 3.50 GHz MacBook Pro, 16 GB LPDDR3
tradeoffs: Single C99 header, usable from C++; clips cell edges for you, exposes cell edge lists, supports Delaunay generation and custom allocators. Boost.Polygon's Voronoi handles segment sites; this library is point sites only.
caveats: The Boost ratio is stated in prose as relative to 'the fastest algorithms' (Fastjet and jcv), not as a direct jcv vs Boost figure. The result charts and test/report.md linked from the README returned 404, compiler and flags are not stated, and the machine is a 2017 laptop. The README's numbers section is old; the repo's current benchmark tooling (benchmark/, Benchmarks.md) targets WebAssembly vs d3-delaunay, not Boost. Boost.Polygon is not Boost.Geometry.
found_via: GitHub: JCash/voronoi README 'Some Numbers' and 'General thoughts' sections (surfaced while checking Voronoi libraries vs Boost.Polygon)

name: DGtal QuickHull
workload: 3D convex hull computation (QuickHull class in src/DGtal/geometry/tools/QuickHull.h, arbitrary dimension, exact lattice-point kernel available).
claimed_speedup: Source doc comment: 'This version is generally more than twice faster than CGAL convex_hull_3 for the usual CGAL kernels Cartesian and Exact_predicates_inexact_constructions_kernel.' No timings in the file.
tradeoffs: Part of the DGtal digital-geometry library, so using it pulls in DGtal and its dependencies. Facets are not necessarily triangles/simplices in the output, unlike CGAL's simplicial hull. Kernel is selectable, with an exact integral kernel for lattice points. Not tailored for incremental or dynamic hulls. LGPL.
caveats: A single qualitative sentence in a code comment with no methodology, point counts, hardware or flags; the DGtal docs page that repeats it (module QuickHull) could not be opened. Only the 3D convex hull is claimed faster; the higher-dimensional and Delaunay-cell uses have no baseline.
found_via: WebSearch 'convex hull C++ library benchmark faster than CGAL Qhull github README' (DGtal docs snippet), then read QuickHull.h on raw.githubusercontent.com

name: Indexicon
workload: R-tree insertion time and range-query time across node capacities 32 to 512 on six datasets (MARINE, MIAMI, OSM, TAXIS, TIGER, TORONTO), Indexicon R-tree vs Boost R-tree.
claimed_speedup: README figures only (no table). Read off the charts (derived from page data): range query up to about 1.5x faster, e.g. MARINE at capacity 32 about 425 ms Boost vs about 280 ms Indexicon, TORONTO at capacity 32 about 39 ms vs about 30 ms; insertion about 5-20% faster, e.g. MARINE at capacity 512 about 32 s vs about 25 s; TIGER and low-capacity insertion are near parity.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the benchmark; README test build uses g++ -std=c++17 -O2
tradeoffs: Single-header R-tree (top-down packing, R* insertion, deletion with orphan reinsertion), quad-tree, MX-CIF quad-tree, oct-tree and kd-tree behind one API; point and MBB data. Less generic than Boost.Geometry (no arbitrary geometry types or strategies).
caveats: Only chart images in the README; benchmark driver code is not in the repository (figures/ holds results, test/ holds examples), CPU and benchmark flags are not given, and Boost version is not stated. The paper (arXiv 2606.04676) with the comprehensive benchmark could not be opened (arXiv blocked), so it is a preprint claim at best. Gains are modest for an R-tree and shrink or vanish in some configurations.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/spatial-index?l=c++ (also listed as a lead from earlier geo searches)

name: Coal (HPP-FCL)
baseline: FCL (Flexible Collision Library) GJK; also Bullet GJK and libccd (MPR and GJK)
workload: Narrow-phase convex collision and distance queries: per-query time distribution (microseconds, log scale) of Coal's GJK, Polyak-accelerated GJK and Nesterov-accelerated GJK versus FCL, Bullet and libccd.
claimed_speedup: README: the accelerated GJK variants 'largely outperform by a large margin (from 5x up to 15x times faster)'. From the README box plot (derived from page data): median about 1.1 us (Nesterov), 1.2 us (Polyak), 1.6 us (Coal GJK) vs about 4.2 us (libccd MPR and GJK), about 9.5 us (FCL GJK), about 17 us (Bullet GJK).
stars_or_usage: 645 stars; used by Pinocchio, Humanoid Path Planner and Simple
tradeoffs: Python bindings; adds safety margins, contact points and patches, serialization (Boost.Serialization), more shape types (height fields, capsules, ellipsoids). Narrow-phase focus; the project descends from FCL (renamed from HPP-FCL in 2024).
caveats: README chart only: hardware, compiler, flags and the benchmark harness are not stated and no benchmark directory is visible in the repo; the RSS 2022 paper that backs the Nesterov/Polyak results was not opened. Baseline FCL is not in the category's list (Boost.Geometry, CGAL, GEOS, R-tree), and collision detection is only loosely 'geometry-spatial'. The 5x to 15x range is the README's, the medians above are my reading of the chart.
found_via: GitHub: coal-library/coal README 'A high-performance library' section (found while checking collision-detection libraries)

name: libnabo
baseline: ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor library, Mount and Arya)
workload: K-nearest-neighbour search in low-dimensional spaces (kd-tree), as used for ICP shape registration.
claimed_speedup: README: 'On the average, libnabo is 5% to 20% faster than ANN.' No table; `make test` runs comparative benchmarks if ANN or FLANN are installed.
tradeoffs: Depends on Eigen (2 or 3); optional Boost for Python bindings. Scalar-type-agnostic templates; the CPU kd-tree is strongly inspired by ANN with more compact data types.
caveats: One sentence with no numbers beyond the 5-20% range, no hardware, flags or dataset. The README points to Elseberg et al., JOSER 2012 for the evaluation; that paper was not opened. Gains are small. Baseline ANN is not in the category's list.
found_via: GitHub: norlab-ulaval/libnabo README (nearest-neighbor kd-tree libraries check)

name: kd3
workload: kd-tree build time and k-NN query throughput (k=1 and k=10, 100,000 queries) on 11 point-cloud datasets (autzen LiDAR, bunny, dragon, cities, synthetic blobs, sphere shell, torus, solid, anisotropic, powerlaw, mixture) in four kd3 configurations (base, aabb, fast, fast-aabb), validated against brute force.
claimed_speedup: README: k-NN queries 'in most scenarios are significantly faster compared to nanoflann'. From the committed CSV (assets/results/5950X/kd3_datasets_report.csv, 132 rows, ratios derived from page data): median build 3.7x faster (range 0.22x-6.42x); median query throughput 1.86x of nanoflann (range 0.01x-5.05x); aabb and fast-aabb configs about 1.7x-2.9x median, on-cloud queries with the fast config up to 5.05x. Example row: autzen, 5M points, k=10, on-cloud: 511,698 vs 295,318 queries/s, build 0.086 s vs 0.416 s.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (xmake release build; README advises profile-guided optimization)
hardware: Workstation with a '5950X' CPU (results directory name; exact model and thread count not stated)
tradeoffs: Header-only, small key dimension (2-4 ideal), SoA SIMD leaves, OpenMP build, zero-allocation traversal, non-owning view suitable for GPU offload, C API, GLSL generator. AGPL-3.0 network copyleft limits use in closed products. Not the most complete or flexible kd-tree library.
caveats: Mixed result: 39 of 132 CSV rows are slower than nanoflann, mostly the 'base' configuration on uniform-in-bounding-box queries (median 0.32x-0.40x), which is why the aabb configurations exist. Compiler, flags and exact CPU are not stated, no independent reproduction. Very young repo (first visible commit May 2026) with 11 stars. Baseline nanoflann is not Boost.Geometry/CGAL/GEOS.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/kdtree?l=c++ (kd3 README and committed benchmark CSV)

name: kigumi
baseline: CGAL Polygon_mesh_processing corefinement ('coref.'); also libigl igl::copyleft::cgal::mesh_boolean (CGAL exact), geogram, Manifold, MCUT
workload: Boolean intersection of two triangle meshes, excluding I/O, on four generated mesh pairs (open, open and closed, closed, non-manifold); wall-clock seconds.
claimed_speedup: README table (seconds): Closed: CGAL coref. 27.2 vs kigumi 4.6 sequential (about 5.9x, derived) and 1.1 parallel; libigl (CGAL exact) 39.3. Open: coref. 3.2 vs kigumi 2.4 sequential (about 1.3x, derived) and 0.6 parallel. Open and closed, and non-manifold: CGAL coref. FAILED, kigumi 1.0/0.4 and 0.5/0.1 s. Manifold is faster on closed meshes (1.3 s sequential, 0.2 s parallel) but approximate.
compiler_and_flags: Homebrew Clang 22.1.1, CMake Release build (./run configure uses -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release; explicit -O flags not stated); benchmark programs in benches/, driven by tools/run_benches.sh and tools/gen_bench_meshes.sh
tradeoffs: Header-only; needs a CGAL-compatible kernel and 2D triangulation (LGPL and GPL-or-commercial CGAL packages), so using it brings CGAL's license terms. Exact predicates and constructions, open/closed/non-manifold meshes, nested regions, per-face data. Inputs must be free of degenerate faces and self-intersections. Based on Barki et al. 2015 with optimizations.
caveats: Mesh sizes, CGAL and libigl versions and the exact meshes are not stated in the README (meshes are generated by a script in the repo), and the build flags are only implicit in CMake Release, so the A tier is borderline. The 'Open' sequential gain over CGAL is only 1.3x. Manifold beats kigumi on the closed case but is approximate. Single machine (Apple M4). MIT code, but the CGAL dependency makes the combined work LGPL/GPL.

name: Polylidar3D
baseline: CGAL 2D Alpha Shapes (also PostGIS ST_ConcaveHull 2.5.2 and Spatialite ST_ConcaveHull, which the README treats as GEOS-based)
workload: Non-convex (concave hull) polygon extraction from random point sets sampled inside the California state outline, 2,000 to about 64,000 points, with and without holes; execution time in ms (concavehull-evaluation repo).
claimed_speedup: Chart in the concavehull-evaluation README (no table): at about 64,000 points Polylidar is roughly 30 ms, CGAL alpha shapes roughly 190-200 ms, PostGIS roughly 3,100 ms (solid line) and Spatialite roughly 11,300 ms; i.e. about 6x faster than CGAL, 100x or more than PostGIS and Spatialite (values read from the chart, derived from page data). The repo also notes that robust predicates are enabled for the comparison and that disabling them gives a further 30% speedup.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated (C++14 compiler; Polylidar built with PL_USE_ROBUST_PREDICATES=1; CGAL 4.12, PostGIS 2.5.2)
tradeoffs: C++ with pybind11 Python bindings; multi-threading (marl) and optional GPU path in the 3D mode; polygons with holes. It extracts planar-region polygons from Delaunay-triangulated data, so the hull is defined differently from an alpha shape or PostGIS concave hull; CGAL returns unordered boundary edges rather than a polygon.
caveats: The evidence is a chart image in a separate benchmark repo (4 stars), with no hardware, flags, or table; the CGAL timing only covers alpha shape construction plus boundary edge extraction and excludes making a polygon. The peer-reviewed paper (Castagno and Atkins, IEEE RA-L 2020) was not opened, so there is no B-tier confirmation. CGAL 4.12 is old. Repo is unmaintained since 2023-03.
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/polygon?l=c++ (Polylidar), then its linked JeremyBYU/concavehull-evaluation repo

name: detria
baseline: CDT (artem-ogre/CDT) and poly2tri; Triangle (CMU) is also in the comparison but is faster on random point sets
workload: Constrained Delaunay triangulation timing (set-up and result retrieval excluded) on Natural Earth country outlines, poly2tri test files, a cocircular fractal, and 1,000 to 1,000,000 random points inside a square; box plots of repeated runs.
claimed_speedup: Medians printed in the per-case SVG result files (images/benchmark/*.svg, embedded in BENCHMARKS.md; detria vs CDT vs Triangle, ms): world land outline (407,072 vertices) 502 vs 1431 vs 441; United States outline 24.4 vs 58.8 vs 27.2; Afghanistan (1,532 vertices) 0.74 vs 2.17 vs 0.87; 10,000-vertex debug2.dat 11.6 vs 28.7 vs 12.5. Tallied over the 23 result files: faster than CDT in 21 of 23 cases (about 1.5x to 3.2x), faster than poly2tri in all 14 cases it supports, faster than Triangle in 16 of 23 (country outlines, city.dat, debug2.dat). Slower than Triangle on random points (1,000,000 points: 1798 vs 946 ms) and the world land outline (502 vs 441 ms), and slower than both Triangle and CDT on the cocircular fractals of depth 6 and 8 (depth 8: 3091 vs 1407 CDT vs 857 Triangle).
compiler_and_flags: Clang 17.0.3 (MSVC-like command line), release build with default compiler flags
tradeoffs: Single-header CDT with a C# port; no point insertion after triangulation, no Steiner or refinement (stated non-goal). CDT and poly2tri versions are not stated. Triangle is still faster for generic point sets.
caveats: Mixed result: the library wins against CDT and poly2tri on most inputs, wins against Triangle only on country-outline style inputs, and loses to Triangle on random points and fractals and to CDT on the deep fractals. The A tier rests on 'default compiler flags' of a release build, which is vague. Baseline versions are not stated, the machine is a 2019 desktop on Windows, and neither CDT nor poly2tri is the category's incumbent (CGAL, Boost.Geometry, GEOS are not compared).
found_via: GitHub topic page github.com/topics/delaunay-triangulation?l=c++&o=desc&s=updated; BENCHMARKS.md result SVGs parsed for the median values
